p.src: Pilgrim sprang into the air, leaped across the Eastern Ocean, and soon reached the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He lowered his cloud and looked about with eyes wide open. All the flowers and grasses on the mountain were gone, and every trace of rosy mist had vanished; the peaks and crags had collapsed, and the woods were scorched and withered. How had it come to this? It was because, after he had thrown Heaven into turmoil and been taken up to the celestial realm, the Illustrious Sage Erlang had led the Seven Brothers of Mount Mei here and burned the mountain to ruin. The Great Sage was more desolate than ever. As testimony, there is an old-style ballad on the ruined mountain and its desolate scene. The ballad says:

p.src: As the Great Sage grieved, he suddenly heard a sound from a hollow thick with vitex bushes before the fragrant-grass slope. Seven or eight little monkeys sprang out, rushed forward together, surrounded him, and kowtowed. They cried aloud, “Grandfather Great Sage, have you come home today?” The Handsome Monkey King said, “Why are none of you playing about? Why is every one of you hiding out of sight? I have been here quite some time without seeing hide or hair of you. Why is that?” At this, the monkeys shed tears one after another and told him, “Ever since the Great Sage was seized and taken to the upper realm, we have suffered unbearably at the hands of hunters. How could we withstand their stout crossbows and powerful bows, their hawks and vicious hounds, their nets, snares, spears, and hooks? So, valuing our lives, we dared not come out to play, but hid deep in caves and kept far away in secluded dens. When hungry, we steal grass from the slope; when thirsty, we drink clear water below in the ravine. Just now we heard Grandfather Great Sage’s voice and came especially to greet you. We beg you to protect us.” When the Great Sage heard this, his sorrow deepened still further. He asked, “How many of you are still on this mountain?” The monkeys replied, “Old and young together, only about a thousand.” The Great Sage said, “I once had forty-seven thousand demons under me. Where have they all gone now?” The monkeys said, “After Grandfather left, Bodhisattva Erlang set fire to this mountain, and more than half were burned to death. We survived by crouching in wells, burrowing into the ravines, and hiding beneath the Iron Slab Bridge. By the time the fire had died and the smoke dispersed and we came out again, there were no flowers or fruit to sustain us. We could scarcely survive, so another half went elsewhere. The half of us who remained have endured hardship here in the mountain. And over these last two years, hunters have carried off half of us yet again.” Pilgrim asked, “Why do they carry you off?” The monkeys said, “Those hunters are hateful beyond words! Those of us struck by arrows or stabbed by spears, poisoned or beaten to death, they carry away, skin and bone, then simmer in sauce, steam with vinegar, fry in oil, or sauté with salt, making us into dishes to eat with their rice. Others caught in nets or snares are taken alive and taught to leap through hoops, perform tricks, turn somersaults, and stand on their hands. They beat gongs and drums with us in the streets and make us perform every sort of antic.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Great Sage grew even more furious and asked, “Who is still in charge inside the cave?” The demons replied, “Marshals Ma and Liu and Generals Beng and Ba are still managing things.” The Great Sage said, “Go and tell them that I have returned.” The little demons rushed through the entrance and reported, “Grandfather Great Sage has come home!” When Ma, Liu, Beng, and Ba heard the news, they hurried out, kowtowed, and welcomed him into the cave. The Great Sage sat in the center while all the monsters bowed before him and said, “Grandfather Great Sage, we recently heard that your life had been spared and that you were protecting the Tang Monk on his journey west to fetch the scriptures. Why have you turned back to your own mountain instead of continuing west?” The Great Sage said, “Little ones, you do not understand. That Tang Sanzang cannot tell the worthy from the wicked. All along the road I caught monsters and subdued demons for him, exhausted every skill I had learned in my life, and slew fiends time and again; but he said I was committing violence and evil, refused to keep me as his disciple, and drove me back here. He even wrote a letter of dismissal as proof that he would never employ me again.”

p.src: The monkeys clapped their hands and laughed. “What good fortune! What good fortune! Why be a monk? Come home and lead us in merrymaking for a few years!” They called, “Quickly, prepare coconut wine to welcome Grandfather home!” The Great Sage said, “No wine yet. Tell me, how often do those hunters come to our mountain?” Ma and Liu replied, “Great Sage, they have no fixed time. They come here and harass us every single day.” The Great Sage asked, “Why have they not come today?” Ma and Liu said, “They will probably be here soon.” The Great Sage ordered, “Little ones, all of you go out and gather up the fire-brittled stones scattered over the mountain, then pile them here for me. Make some heaps of twenty or thirty stones and others of fifty or sixty. I have a use for them.” The little monkeys swarmed out like bees, each haphazardly carrying stones until they had gathered many heaps. After inspecting them, the Great Sage said, “Little ones, hide yourselves inside the cave and let Old Sun work his magic.”

p.src: The Great Sage lowered his cloud, clapped his hands, and laughed. “What good fortune! What good fortune! Ever since I submitted to the Tang Monk and became a monk myself, he has repeatedly admonished me, saying, ‘Though one does good for a thousand days, one’s goodness is still insufficient; but if one does evil for a single day, one’s evil is already more than enough.’ There is indeed truth in those words. While I followed him, I killed only a few demons, yet he blamed me for committing violence. But today, on returning home, I have finished off all these hunters.” He called, “Little ones, come out!” When the fierce wind had passed and the monkeys heard the Great Sage calling, they leaped out one after another. The Great Sage said, “Go to the foot of the southern mountain, strip the clothes from the dead hunters, bring them home, wash away the bloodstains, and wear them against the cold; push all the dead men’s bodies into that fathomless pool; drag back the fallen horses, skin them and make boots from the hides, then salt the meat and eat it at your leisure; use the bows, arrows, spears, and swords to drill yourselves in martial arts; and gather up all their motley banners for my use.” The monkeys all accepted his orders.

p.src: The Great Sage took the banners apart and washed them, then stitched them all together into one great multicolored standard. Upon it he wrote fourteen characters: “The Mountain of Flowers and Fruit Restored, the Water Curtain Cave Reestablished, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.” He raised a pole and hung the banner outside the cave. Day after day he summoned demons and gathered beasts, stockpiling fodder and provisions, without another word about being a “monk.” So wide was his influence and so great his power that he went to the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas and borrowed sweet rain and celestial water, with which he washed the mountain green again. Elms and willows were planted in front, pines and nanmu trees behind, and there was no lack of peaches, plums, jujubes, or flowering plums. Thereafter they lived free and easy, content in their occupations and peaceful in their homes; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Tang Sanzang, deceived by the fiend's cunning, had cast off the unruly ape; he mounted and set out. Bajie opened the way ahead, while Friar Sand carried the luggage westward. After crossing White Tiger Ridge, they suddenly came upon a stretch of wooded hills, truly a place of clinging vines and entwining creepers, green cypresses and verdant pines. Sanzang called out, “Disciples, the mountain path is rugged and exceedingly hard to travel. These pine woods are dense and the trees stand thick on every side. You must be very careful, lest there be evil spirits or savage beasts.” See how that fool roused his spirits, told Friar Sand to lead the horse, and used his rake to clear a path, guiding Tang Sanzang straight into the pine forest. As they went on, the elder reined in his horse and said, “Bajie, I truly have grown hungry today. Where can you find some vegetarian food for me?” Bajie replied, “Master, please dismount and wait here while Old Pig goes to look.” The elder dismounted, and Friar Sand set down the carrying pole, took out the begging bowl, and handed it to Bajie. Bajie said, “Off I go.” The elder asked, “Where are you going?” Bajie replied, “Never mind that. I shall bore through ice to fetch fire if I must, and press snow for oil, but I will return with alms enough for a meal.”

p.src: See how he left the pine forest and traveled more than ten li westward without encountering a single household. It was truly a place with wolves and tigers but no trace of man. The fool had walked until he was weary and pondered to himself, “When Brother Monkey was with us, whatever the old monk wanted, he got at once; but now that the task has fallen to me, the saying proves true: ‘Only the keeper of a household knows the price of fuel and rice; only one who raises children understands the kindness of parents.’ In all fairness, there is nowhere to beg for food.” Then drowsiness overtook him, and he thought, “If I go straight back and tell the old monk there was nowhere to beg for food, he will not believe that I have walked so far. I had better idle away another hour or so before going back to report. Very well, very well—I shall have a little sleep in this patch of grass.” The fool thrust his head into the grass and lay down to sleep. At first he intended only to doze briefly and then rise, but how could he know that a man worn out from walking, once his head is down, will simply begin snoring away?

p.src: For now, we shall leave Bajie sleeping there. We turn instead to the elder in the forest, whose ears burned and eyes twitched, leaving him uneasy in body and mind. He hastily turned and called to Friar Sand, “Wuneng went to beg for food. Why has he not returned after all this time?” Friar Sand replied, “Master, you still do not understand him. He knows that many households in the Western Regions feed wandering monks, and his belly is enormous. Do you think he cares about you? He will not return until he has eaten his fill.” Sanzang said, “That is true. If he is lingering there, engrossed in eating, how are we to meet up with him? Night is falling, and this is no place to stay. We must find lodgings somewhere.” Friar Sand said, “Do not worry, Master. Sit here awhile, and I shall go find him.” Sanzang said, “Yes, yes. Whether there is food or not no longer matters; finding a place to stay is the urgent thing.” Friar Sand snatched up his precious staff and went straight out of the pine forest to look for Bajie.

p.src: Left sitting alone in the forest, the elder grew exceedingly bored and weary. He had no choice but to summon his spirits, spring to his feet, gather the luggage in one place, and tether the horse to a tree. He removed the rain hat from his head, planted his priest's staff upright, straightened his black robe, and strolled slowly through the secluded woods to dispel his gloom. The elder looked over all the wild grasses and mountain flowers, yet could not bear the clamor of birds returning to their nests. The forest was full of places where the grass grew deep and the paths were narrow. His thoughts being in turmoil, he took the wrong way. For one thing, he wished to relieve his boredom; for another, he wanted to find Bajie and Friar Sand. Unexpectedly, while the two disciples had gone due west, the elder wandered about for a time and turned south instead. Emerging from the pine forest, he suddenly raised his head and saw golden light flashing and multicolored vapors rising in the distance. Looking closely, he saw that it was a precious pagoda whose golden roof shone with light. It was the light of the setting sun in the west reflecting brightly from the golden roof. He said, “My disciples have no affinity with the faith after all. Ever since leaving the Eastern Land, I have vowed to burn incense whenever I encounter a temple, bow to every Buddha I see, and sweep every pagoda I meet. Is that shining structure not a golden pagoda? Why did they not take that road? There must be a monastery beneath the pagoda, and monks within the monastery. I shall go and see. As for the luggage and the white horse, no one appears to travel through this place, so they should come to no harm. If there is lodging there, I shall wait until my disciples return, and we can all ask to rest the night together.”

p.src: When the elder saw its dreadful appearance, he recoiled in terror. His whole body went numb, and his legs grew weak and sore; he hastily turned to flee. He had barely turned around when the demon—whose spiritual senses were truly keen—opened wide a pair of golden, ghostly eyes and shouted, “Little ones! See who is outside the gate!” One little demon poked its head out and looked beyond the gate. Seeing a bald-headed elder, it hurried back inside and reported, “Great King, there is a monk outside. He has a round head and broad face, with earlobes hanging to his shoulders; his whole body is covered in tender flesh, and his skin is fine and delicate. What an excellent monk he is!” Hearing this, the demon laughed aloud and said, “This is what they call ‘a fly landing on a snake's head—food delivering itself to the door.’ All of you, hurry after him and seize him for me. I shall reward you handsomely.” The little demons surged forward together like a swarm of bees. When Sanzang saw them, his anxious heart flew swift as an arrow and his feet raced as though on wings; yet terror made his courage fail, and his legs and feet were weak and numb. Moreover, the mountain path was rugged, the forest deep, and the sun setting. How could he move quickly? The little demons caught him and carried him off bodily. Just as the verse says:

p.src: See how the little demons carried the elder to the bamboo curtain, set him down outside it, and joyfully announced, “Great King, we have brought in the monk!” The old demon stole a glance and saw Tripitaka standing erect, with a stately countenance—a truly fine monk. He thought to himself, “A monk as fine as this must be a person of high standing, not one to be taken lightly. Unless I make an imposing show, how will he ever submit to me?” All at once, borrowing another’s might to bolster his own, he made his red whiskers bristle, his blood-red hair stand on end, and his eyes bulge, then roared, “Bring that monk in!” All the demons answered loudly together, “Yes!” Then they gave Tripitaka a hard shove inside. As the saying goes, “Once beneath a low eave, how dare one not bow one’s head?” Tripitaka could only press his palms together and salute him. The demon asked, “Where are you a monk from? Where have you come from? Where are you going? Explain yourself at once!” Tripitaka replied, “I am a monk of the Tang court. By command of the Great Tang emperor, I am journeying to the Western Heaven to seek the scriptures and sacred verses. Passing through your honored mountain, I came especially to pay homage to the holy presence beneath the pagoda. I did not expect to disturb Your Majesty and beg forgiveness. When I have obtained the scriptures in the West and returned to the Eastern Land, I shall record your illustrious name forever.” Hearing this, the demon laughed aloud. “I said you must be a person from the superior realm, and indeed it is you. I have been wanting to eat you, and how very fortunate that you have come! Otherwise, might I not have let you slip by? You are destined to be food for my mouth, so naturally you came stumbling straight to me. Even if I released you, you could not get away; even if you ran, you could not escape!” He called to the little demons, “Take that monk away and bind him!” Sure enough, the little demons swarmed forward, wound ropes and cords around the elder, and bound him to the Soul-Fixing Post.

p.src: Holding his blade, the old demon asked again, “Monk, how many are in your party? Surely you would not dare go to the Western Heaven alone?” Seeing the blade, Tripitaka answered honestly, “Great King, I have two disciples named Zhu Bajie and Friar Sand. Both have gone out of the pine forest to beg for food. There is also a load of luggage and a white horse, both left in the pine forest.” The old demon said, “What further good fortune! Two disciples, three with you, and four with the horse—that is enough for one meal.” A little demon said, “We will go and capture them.” The old demon said, “Do not go out. Shut the front gate. When those two return from begging for food, they are certain to look for their master so that he may eat. Unable to find him, they are certain to come searching at my gate. As the saying goes, ‘Business that comes to your door is easily done.’ Let us wait and catch them at our leisure.” The little demons closed the front gate.

p.src: For now, we shall say no more of Tripitaka’s calamity. We turn instead to Friar Sand, who left the forest in search of Bajie. He went a good ten li or more without seeing a single village or hamlet. As he stood on a high mound looking about, he suddenly heard someone speaking in the grass. He hurriedly parted the thick grass with his staff and looked, only to find the Idiot inside, talking in his sleep. Only when Friar Sand seized him by the ear did he wake up. Friar Sand said, “You fine idiot! Master sent you to beg for food—did he give you leave to sleep here?” The Idiot awoke with a start and said, “Brother, what time is it?” Friar Sand said, “Get up quickly. Master said it no longer matters whether we have food or not; he told you and me to find a place to stay.”

p.src: Still muddled with sleep, the Idiot held his alms bowl and gripped his rake, then went straight back with Friar Sand. When they reached the forest and looked, their master was gone. Friar Sand complained, “It is all because you, Idiot, failed to return with food. Some demon must have taken Master.” Bajie laughed. “Brother, do not talk nonsense. That forest is a peaceful and elegant place; there certainly cannot be any demons there. The old monk probably grew restless and went off somewhere to look around. Let us go and find him.” The two had no choice but to lead the horse and shoulder the luggage. Gathering up the cloak and priest’s staff, they left the pine forest to search for their master.

p.src: As it happened, the Tang Monk was not fated to die this time. After searching for a while without finding him, the two suddenly saw golden light flashing due south. Bajie said, “Brother, a blessed man is blessed indeed! Look, Master has gone to that household. That shining thing is a precious pagoda. Who would dare neglect him there? They must have prepared a vegetarian meal and kept him there to enjoy it. Let us quicken our steps and catch up so that we too may eat some.” Friar Sand said, “Brother, we cannot yet tell whether this bodes good or ill. Let us go and see.”

p.src: The two strode boldly up to the gate. “Ah! It is shut.” Above the gate they saw a slab of white jade set crosswise, engraved with six large characters: “Wave-Moon Cave, Bowl Mountain.” Friar Sand said, “Brother, this is no monastery. It is a demon’s cave. Even if our master is here, we will not be allowed to see him.” Bajie said, “Do not be afraid, brother. Tether the horse and guard the luggage while I ask them for news.” The Idiot raised his rake, stepped forward, and shouted, “Open the gate! Open the gate!” A gatekeeping demon inside the cave opened the gate. The moment he saw what the two looked like, he drew back at once, ran inside, and reported, “Great King, business has come to our door!” The old demon asked, “What business?” The little demon replied, “Outside the cave gate are a long-snouted, big-eared monk and another monk with a gloomy complexion. They have come calling at the gate.” The old demon was delighted. “It is Zhu Bajie and Friar Sand, come searching this way. Well! They know how to search, do they? How did they come straight to my gate? Since they look fierce and unruly, we must not take them lightly.” He called out, “Bring me my armor!” The little demons brought it over. He dressed himself, took up his blade, and went straight out through the gate.

p.src: The old Yellow-Robed Monster came through the gate and asked, “What monks are you, and why are you shouting at my door?” Bajie replied, “My boy, do you not recognize me? I am your grandfather. I was sent by the Great Tang to journey to the Western Heaven. My master is Tripitaka, the emperor’s sworn younger brother. If he is in your house, send him out at once and spare me the trouble of smashing my way in with this rake.” The monster laughed. “Yes, yes, yes! There is a Tang monk in my house. I have not neglected him either; I have prepared some buns stuffed with human flesh for him to eat. Why do you two not come in and have one as well?”
